summary: A 1975 note about the problem of junk mail on the ARPANET, unwanted messages that fill up users' mailboxes. It is an early discussion of what we now call spam.

plainLanguage.summary: Junk mail is not new. Even on the earliest network people got messages they did not want, and this note talks about it.

subtitle: An early call to filter unwanted messages on the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET Host/IMP interface protocol has no way for a Host to refuse incoming messages. A misbehaving Host could send many messages to another Host, wasting processor time and network bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: A Host could tell its IMP to refuse messages from specific source Hosts. The IMP would either filter locally or forward the refusal notice upstream to the source IMP for broader filtering.
tldr.outcome: Allowing selective message refusal would give Hosts a practical defense against misbehaving senders without requiring protocol changes at higher layers.

today: RFC 706 is one of the earliest discussions of what we now call spam filtering. The problem of unwanted messages persists today, though the mechanisms for blocking have evolved considerably.

sections.title: The Junk Mail Problem
sections.content: The ARPANET Host/IMP interface protocol provides no mechanism for a Host to selectively refuse messages. If a Host wants to receive any particular messages, it must read and examine all messages sent to it. This design opens the door to denial of service: a malfunctioning Host could bombard another Host with messages, consuming processor time and network bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: On the early ARPANET, if a computer got flooded with unwanted messages, there was no way to tell the network to stop delivering them.

sections.title: Selective Message Refusal
sections.content:
Postel proposes adding a capability to the Host/IMP interface so that a Host can tell its IMP: "refuse messages from Host X". The IMP would then discard unwanted messages at the earliest opportunity and return a refusal notice to the offending Host.

Two implementation approaches are sketched. In the first, the destination IMP maintains a per-Host list of refused sources and filters locally. In the second, the destination IMP forwards the refusal notice upstream to the source IMP, which maintains per-Host lists of refused destinations, spreading the filtering load.

A Host could measure incoming message rates per source and, if a threshold is exceeded, issue a refusal command to its IMP. The refusal could be revoked later by an accept command or by resetting the Host/IMP interface.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer should be able to tell its IMP: "Do not let messages from Host X through." The IMP could filter them away or tell that Host to stop.

sections.title: Benefit
sections.content: This mechanism would protect Hosts from wasteful message floods without requiring changes to application protocols or Host operating systems. The filtering happens at the network edge, where it can be most efficient.
sections.plainLanguage: This solves the problem at the network level, before the messages waste the recipient's computer power.
